Juvenile recruitment in the Dusky sweeper Pempheris adusta begins with the emergence of planktonic larvae whose initial body mass is remarkably low. Newly hatched individuals, having just undergone eclosion from a demersal egg, possess a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams]. This minuscule mass reflects the energetic constraints of a pelagic larval phase that relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days of development. Field surveys of the study population conducted near coral reef habitats in the Indo-Pacific indicate that the onset of exogenous feeding typically occurs within 48 hours following hatching, after which larvae commence active planktivory. The rapid depletion of the yolk sac during this lecithotrophic stage is a critical bottleneck for survival, as larvae must successfully transition to capturing zooplankton before their energy reserves are exhausted. Comparative data from related pempherid species suggest that this brief dependence on maternally derived nutrients is common among sweepers, though the exact timing of first feeding can vary with local water temperature and prey availability.

As individuals progress through the juvenile phase, they undergo substantial somatic growth before reaching the size threshold associated with sexual maturation. For Pempheris adusta, the standard length at puberty has been estimated from dissected specimens at 7.66 centimeters [Lp = 7.66 centimeters]. This measurement corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 7 grams [Wwp = approximately 7 grams], based on length-weight regressions derived from the same collection series. The attainment of puberty marks the point at which gametogenesis commences, a transition confirmed histologically by the presence of developing oocytes in females and spermatogenic cysts in males. Juveniles typically occupy shallow, structurally complex microhabitats such as rocky overhangs and sponge aggregations, where they benefit from reduced predation pressure and abundant small invertebrate prey. The time required to reach this pubertal size varies among individuals, but available growth increment data from otolith readings indicate that most fish attain 7.66 centimeters standard length within their first twelve to eighteen months of life under ambient reef conditions.

The reproductive biology of the Dusky sweeper has been characterized through both field sampling and laboratory-based observations on captive individuals. At a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], females produce approximately 13,000 eggs per year, distributed across multiple spawning events, with gravid individuals captured during peak breeding months showing asynchronous oocyte development consistent with batch spawning. The high fecundity, typical of many small-bodied teleosts with pelagic eggs, offsets substantial early-life mortality during the planktonic larval phase. Reproductive adults aggregate in loose schools near cave entrances and under ledges during dusk hours, a behavior that may facilitate synchronized gamete release and enhance fertilization success. The maximum recorded adult size in the sampled population, representing the ultimate standard length, reaches 17 centimeters [Li = 17 centimeters], which corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 76 grams [Wwi = approximately 76 grams] based on the species-specific length-mass relationship. Individuals attaining this size are observed infrequently and likely represent the oldest and most experienced members of the population.

Longevity estimates for Pempheris adusta derive primarily from the analysis of a large, multi-year capture-mark-recapture dataset. The oldest individual documented during the 15-year study period, a female collected from a submerged cave system off the coast of Okinawa, was determined to be 5,840 days [am = 5,840 days] old based on validated otolith increment counts at the prevailing water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This age makes the Dusky sweeper one of the longer-lived members of the Pempheridae family. The advanced age of this specimen is notable given that many reef-associated planktivores typically exhibit shorter lifespans, a pattern that suggests the species may occupy a relatively low-mortality ecological niche. Fish of this age also display the largest body sizes recorded in the population, with several exceeding 15 centimeters standard length. The maximum life span is likely greater than the 5,840 days recorded, as the sampling gear preferentially captured smaller, younger individuals and may have under-sampled the oldest, most crevice-dwelling adults. Future studies employing otolith microchemistry could further refine these longevity estimates.

The population dynamics of the Dusky sweeper are shaped by the interplay between its high fecundity and its relatively extended life span. The daily reproductive rate of a mature female at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] amounts to approximately 36 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 36 eggs per day], a calculation based on the annual fecundity of approximately 13,000 eggs divided across a 365-day spawning season. This rate is comparable to those reported for other tropical planktivorous fishes that exhibit continuous or near-continuous reproduction throughout the year. The species' iteroparous life history, wherein individuals spawn repeatedly over multiple seasons, buffers the population against sporadic recruitment failures caused by unfavorable oceanographic conditions or predator outbreaks. Juvenile survivorship, though low, benefits from the availability of complex benthic refuge habitats that reduce vulnerability during the vulnerable post-settlement period. Comparative life-history analyses suggest that the combination of small egg size, pelagic larval duration, and moderate adult longevity positions Pempheris adusta as a typical representative of the "periodic" life-history strategy, characterized by high fecundity and delayed reproduction relative to more opportunistic sympatric species.
